issue_context.title: BUG: Handling of NaN values in complex columns
issue_context.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [X] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [X] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [X] I have confirmed this bug exists on the main branch of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([np.nan, 2 + 3j], dtype=np.complex128)

print(s)
print(s.loc[0])
print(s.loc[0] - 1j)
```


### Issue Description

Hi,

I have run into an issue where operations that would give a `NaN` result would be messed up in the case where the column values are a complex `dtype`. The reproducible example linked shows this behavior. The output of this code snippet is:
```
0   N000a000N
1    2.0+3.0j
dtype: complex128
(nan+0j)
(nan-1j)
```

Several issues can be observed here:
1. The value at `s.loc[0]` is `nan +0j`, which is not the expected behavior. One would expect `nan` or `nan + nanj`.
2. The value, when displaying the entire Series (idem for a DataFrame) is displayed as `N000a000N`, which is very confusing at best.
3. The resulting complex number can be subtracted from, as seen in the last output line, giving `nan-1j` where one would still expect `nan` or `nan + nanj`.

It seems here that for a complex dtype entry that should be `nan`, only the real part is made `nan` and the display is messed up. Further down the line, calculations that would normally handle `nan`s will crash (or at least the ones I was running).

**Worth noting**: this is correctly treated as a simple `nan` when calling `s.dropna()`.

### Expected Behavior

The result from the provided code snippet should give `nan` or `nan + nanj`.
The display of the Series should not include any `N000a000N`.

comments:
The behavior is correct. This is how numpy works with complex dtypes, nan is a float, if you want to have the imaginary part as nan as well, then you have to use np.nan + np.nan*0j. 

The display of nan is off though.
This looks to have been fixed on main and IIRC we have tests for this case so closing
